5A

Key ideas

Charge (Q) and current (I)

Definitions

Charge: a property of matter that causes electric effects. Like charges repel, opposite charges attract.
Electron: the lightest stable subatomic particle known. It carries a negative charge of 1.60 × 10−19 coulomb, which is considered the basic unit of electric charge.
Electrical conductor: a material that allows electric charge to flow readily
Electric circuit: the pathway of electrical conductors that allows a continuous loop (or ‘complete circuit’) for electrons to flow through. A circuit with an open switch, or in some other way incomplete, is known as an ‘open’ circuit.
Battery: a source or supply of electrical energy usually formed from a number of electric cells connected in series

5A

Key ideas

Charge (Q) and current (I)

Definitions

Load: the component(s) in a circuit where electrical energy is transformed into other forms of energy, e.g. thermal, light, kinetic energy
Ion: an atom or molecule that carries net positive or negative charge
Current: the net flow of electric charge, measured in amperes (A), where 1 A = 1 C s–1.
Insulator: a material that does not conduct electricity; has few or no free charges
Semiconductor: a material that conducts electricity only partially, or only under certain conditions

Formulas

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, 5A glossary and formula boxes4
5A

Key ideas

Charge (Q) and current (I)

Definitions

Ammeter: an instrument used to measure the electric current in a circuit in amperes (A)
Series: when circuit components are connected one after another in a continuous loop so that the same current passes through each component
Ampere, amp (A): the SI unit for electric current, a fundamental quantity
Coulomb (C): the SI unit for charge. 1 C is equivalent to the combined charge of 6.25 × 108 protons (or electrons) or the amount of charge that passes a point when a current of 1A flows for a time of 1 s.

5A

New knowledgeA useful model of the atom

Charge (Q) and current (I)

As you saw in Chapter 3, an atom can be modelled as a central nucleus composed of protons (positively charged) and neutrons (no charge).

In studying nuclear physics you learnt that protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom are very tightly bound together, so any changes to the nucleus involve very large amounts of energy.

Orbiting the nucleus are electrons (negatively charged), as shown in Figure 5A–2.

Each electron is so tiny that its position at any point in time is difficult to measure.

Figure 5A–2 A useful model (not to scale)of the atom showing a nucleus with protons (red), neutrons (blue) and orbiting electrons (green)
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 5, p. 76
5A

New knowledgeA useful model of the atom

Charge (Q) and current (I)

The outer electrons are involved in chemical bonds (studied in chemistry).

They can sometimes be removed from atoms by friction (experienced on dry days as an electrostatic spark), or by light of sufficient energy (photoelectric effect).

In metals, the outer electrons behave as a ‘sea’ or ‘cloud’ of electrons not bound to any particular nucleus but free to move through the metal, which is called an electrical conductor.

In this chapter you will analyse the behaviour of currents of electrons in electric circuits.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 5, p. 77
5A

New knowledgeCharge and current

Charge (Q) and current (I)

A simple electric circuit consists of a source or supply of electrical energy (e.g. a battery) and a load that converts electrical energy to another form of energy.

They are connected by conductors, usually metal wires, that complete the circuit to make a continuous loop.

The battery is connected at the battery terminals.

In Figure 5A–3, the source is a battery, and the load is a heating coil, but it could be any component that converts electrical energy to a different form.

Figure 5A–3 A simple circuit consisting of a battery and a heating coil of high- resistance metal wire. An electric kettle or coffee machine has a circuit similar to this but uses AC electric current from the mains and a switch. An old- fashioned filament globe is also made of high-resistance wire.
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 5, p. 88
5A

New knowledgeCharge and current

Charge (Q) and current (I)

This load, the electrical heating element, converts most of the electrical energy to thermal energy.

In our model of the metal wires, the outer electrons of the metal atom can move around, like molecules in a liquid (Figure 5A–4 top).

They are called free electrons.

The positive ions are fixed in the metal lattice.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 5, p. 89
5A

New knowledgeCharge and current

Charge (Q) and current (I)

Without the battery, the electrons are constantly moving randomly between ions in the lattice (Figure 5A–4 bottom).

When a battery is connected to each end of the wire, the free electrons drift towards the positive side of the battery, creating a flow or current of electrons (recall that opposite charges attract).

Refer to Figure 5A–5.

As soon as the end of the wire touches the second terminal, there is a complete circuit and current will flow through the wire to the opposite terminal, and through the battery as well.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 5, p. 810
5A

New knowledgeCharge and current

Charge (Q) and current (I)

If the circuit is not a complete loop, no current will flow and it may be called an open circuit.

This drift of electrons is quite slow, about 0.1 mm s–1, because electrons collide with each other and with the positive ions in the metal lattice.

However, the drift begins in all parts of the wire as soon as the connection is made; it is said that ‘the circuit is completed and a current flows’.

The circuit is a complete closed path as the electrons also travel through the battery, then continue on around the circuit again.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 5, p. 811
5A

New knowledgeCharge and current

Charge (Q) and current (I)

The filament immediately begins to heat up as soon as the wires are connected to the battery.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 5, p. 812
5A

New knowledgeConventional current

Charge (Q) and current (I)

Electrons were not discovered until 1897, around 70 years after electric current which by convention was regarded as flowing from positive to negative.

This means that when we refer to ‘current’, we mean the conventional current, which is in the opposite direction to the electron flow.

In physics, the direction of ‘current’ is usually taken as the direction a positive charge would move and is opposite to the direction that electrons (negative charge) actually move in a metal wire (electron current).

The effect the current has (i.e. the energy the current transfers to the load) is the same whether it’s positive (+) or negative (–) charges that move, but it is easiest to remember that ‘current flows from the positive terminal of a battery to the negative terminal’.

Figure 5A–6 Electron current and conventional current, I, flow around a simple circuit containing a battery and a resistive element, in this case an incandescent light globe that converts electrical energy to light (and quite a lot to thermal energy).
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 5, p. 913
5A

New knowledgeConventional current

Charge (Q) and current (I)

From now on, when we refer to ‘current’, we mean conventional current, as if the moving charges are positive.

Any material in which charges are free to flow is a conductor.

Metals contain free electrons, so are good conductors.

In certain circumstances, some gases and liquids also act as conductors.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 5, p. 914
5A

New knowledgeConventional current

Charge (Q) and current (I)

In these cases, there are usually positively and negatively charged ions, both free to move.

When a battery is connected, the positive charges move to the negative terminal and the negative charges drift the opposite way, to the positive terminal.

There are also many materials that have few or no free electrons and do not conduct electricity.

These are known as insulators.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 5, p. 915
5A

New knowledgeConventional current

Charge (Q) and current (I)

Some materials conduct partially or under particular conditions and these are known as semiconductors.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 5, p. 916
5A

New knowledgeAn analogy of electric current

Charge (Q) and current (I)

It is often useful to describe (or ‘model’) something you don’t know about, using its similarities to something familiar.

There are conceptual models, which represent a system people don't understand by relating them to concepts the do understand.

There are mathematical models which describe a system using mathematical equations; and there are physical models, such as small- or large-scale representations of an object.

Of course, there will be similarities and differences in the model compared to the real thing.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 5, p. 1117
5A

New knowledgeAn analogy of electric current

Charge (Q) and current (I)

However, as long as you understand its limits, the model, or ‘analogy’, can be useful to help you understand and even make predictions that can then be tested in the laboratory or even in real life.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 5, p. 1118
5A

New knowledgeBicycle chain analogy

Charge (Q) and current (I)

You can think of a simple electric circuit like the chain on a bicycle.

Imagine the free electrons are the links in the chain.

As soon as the pedals are turned (the battery is connected), every link in the chain begins to move.

The wheel axle will start turning instantly, even though it takes some time for an individual link to travel to the axle cog.

Figure 5A–10 A bicycle chain analogy for an electric circuit
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 5, p. 1119
5A

New knowledgeBicycle chain analogy

Charge (Q) and current (I)

If any part of a circuit is disconnected, the current stops.

This is like when a link in the chain on a bicycle breaks, there is no transfer of energy from the pedals to the axle cog.

When you deliberately start and stop a current, you usually use a switch of some sort to disconnect or ‘open’ the circuit.

Of course, the bicycle chain model has a lot of differences from the real situation, as well as these useful similarities.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 5, p. 1120
5A

New knowledgeBicycle chain analogy

Charge (Q) and current (I)

Electrons are a lot smaller than the chain links and electrons are free to move in three dimensions, not locked into a chain.

Also, the electrical energy carried by each electron is not the same as the kinetic energy of the chain links.

Think of it more as a form of potential energy, like a person carrying a muesli bar to use for energy later.

Many analogies can be used to model electric circuits.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 5, p. 1121
5A

New knowledgeBicycle chain analogy

Charge (Q) and current (I)

They are useful, but of course none of them are truly like the real circuit.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 5, p. 1122
5A

New knowledgeUsing diagrams to represent circuits

Charge (Q) and current (I)

Electric circuits can be simple or complex, but they all consist of the same basic components and follow the same principles in their operation.

To understand a circuit and analyse how it works, you need to identify its component parts and see how they work together to make the circuit operate.

To simplify this, an agreed set of symbols is used in circuit diagrams.

These symbols are used instead of pictures, which could show similar components but not be easily recognised.

Figure 5A–13 Circuit diagrams follow a universal language, to represent circuit components according to their function and connections in the circuit rather than what they look like. Components may be updated or substituted, as long as they perform the same function.
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 5, p. 1323
5A

New knowledgeUsing diagrams to represent circuits

Charge (Q) and current (I)

Symbols are also more compact and quicker to draw.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 5, p. 1324
5A

New knowledgeMeasuring current

Charge (Q) and current (I)

The energy supplied by a battery causes a movement of charge (i.e. an electric current) around a conducting circuit.

The greater the energy supplied by the battery, the greater the current in the circuit, as more electrons flow.

To measure current, an ammeter (from ‘amp-meter’) is placed in the circuit, so that the current to be measured runs through it.

This position is called in series.

Figure 5A–14 An ammeter measures current in the circuit when placed in series, so all the current flowing must pass through it. The circuit is shown in picture format (left) and as a circuit diagram (right). The circuit diagram will be understood by any scientist regardless of what type of battery, cell or ammeter they have access to.
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 5, p. 1525
5A

New knowledgeMeasuring current

Charge (Q) and current (I)

You can think of it as a series of links in a chain, where one component follows another all the way around the circuit with no branches or side-tracks.

The unit for current is the ampere or amp, (A), for short.

One amp is quite a large value of current, so milliamps (mA or 10–3 A) are more often used in laboratory practical work.

To remember ‘in series’, think about a television series where one episode follows another.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 5, p. 1526
5A

New knowledgeCalculating charge from current

Charge (Q) and current (I)

In order to measure charge, a suitable unit is needed.

One possibility is to use, as the basic unit, the amount of charge carried by an electron or a proton.

However, this charge is so tiny that it would be inconvenient for measuring the charges encountered in the laboratory or in everyday life.

In fact, electrons are so tiny (9.1 × 10–31 kg) and have such a small (negative) charge that the unit of charge, the coulomb (C) can be thought of as a large parcel of electrons.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 5, p. 1627
5A

New knowledgeCalculating charge from current

Charge (Q) and current (I)

The coulomb is defined from the amount of current that flows.

The unit of current is the ampere (A): 1 A (1 ampere) = 1 C s–1 (1 coulomb per second) Or, looking at it the other way around, 1 coulomb = the amount of charge passing a point when 1 amp flows for 1 second.

Scientists have agreed to use the coulomb, C, as the unit of charge.

This is quite a large value of charge, so a microcoulomb (μC, 10–6 C) is often used.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 5, p. 1628
5A

New knowledgeCalculating charge from current

Charge (Q) and current (I)

Remember, there are 1 million μC in 1 C.

How many electrons are needed to make up one coulomb of charge?

To answer this, you need to know the size of the charge on an individual electron.

This quantity of charge is known as the elementary or electronic charge, as it has long been regarded as the smallest charge that can be found in nature.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 5, p. 1629
5A

New knowledgeCalculating charge from current

Charge (Q) and current (I)

Some experiments have indicated that smaller charges may exist, but the term ‘elementary charge’ is still used to refer to the charge on an electron.

While the electron carries negative charge, protons carry positive charge of the same magnitude.

The elementary charge, e, equals 1.6 × 10–19 C.

If there are n elementary charges in 1 C, then: n × 1.6 × 10–19 = 1 C Therefore: 1 n= 1 6 10 19 . = 6.25 × 1018 The actual number of electrons in 1 coulomb is 6.25 × 1018.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 5, p. 1630
5A

New knowledgeCalculating charge from current

Charge (Q) and current (I)

This is a very large number!

If the current in a circuit is known, the total charge leaving the battery in a given time interval can be calculated.

The electric current at any point in the circuit is usually given the symbol I.

An equation can be written as follows:

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 5, p. 1631

You trySection 5A questions Q8

Charge (Q) and current (I)
Devise an analogy for electric current that compares electrons to canoeists or kayakers drifting down a river that is flowing gently. a Explain three similarities between this situation and a real electric circuit. b Explain three differences between this situation and a real electric circuit.

Working

a Any three of: The canoeists are all travelling in roughly the same direction and they drift around a bit, just like electrons in a complete circuit. The canoeists on the river are higher at the beginning (upstream) hence higher stored energy, and lower at the end (downstream) hence less stored energy. If there are rapids or other obstacles, the canoeists need to negotiate, the canoeists will spend energy passing through them. b Any three of: Electrons don't have paddles
canoeists can just drift with the current but for electrons the positive ion lattice is stationary, and they drift through it. When canoeists get to the end of their trip, they climb out of the canoe onto the bank, whereas electrons find themselves back at the battery being given more electrical energy and continuing around the circuit again. When canoeists drop down a level through rapids or a small waterfall, they often end up going faster – unlike electrons whose average speed (as measured by the current) doesn't change as they pass around the circuit.

Check-in set 4 · Q1 · 5A
Why is an ammeter always placed *in series* in a circuit? Hint: what does it measure?
An ammeter must be connected in series so that *all* the current in that branch of the circuit passes through the meter, so it all gets counted.
Check-in set 4 · Q2 · 5A
Why do ammeters often have more than one red terminal?
Different connections are for different scales, catering for different currents. Always do a rough calculation of what you expect; begin with the scale that can measure the largest current if in doubt.
Check-in set 4 · Q3 · 5A
Place the ammeter in this circuit so it measures the current. Redraw the circuit diagram to show your solution. Compare your diagram with those of other students. What do you notice? What can you predict about the magnitude of the current in the ammeter, regardless of where placed in the circuit?
Any diagram with the ammeter in series will work. It doesn't matter where in the loop you put the ammeter, as long as it has two connections linked so that the current has to flow through it and can't take a different path. Other students may have their ammeters in a different location.
